questions.text: A decision-tree split has a left child with 2 positive and 0 negative examples and a right child with 2 positive and 2 negative examples. Using Gini=1-p_positive^2-p_negative^2, what is the weighted child Gini?

questions.text: Select ALL correct statements about Python.
options: C. A set stores a separate copy of every repeated value.
D. Assigning a new value to an existing dictionary key updates that entry.
E. Appending to a copied outer list always appends to the original outer list.
questions.explanation: A, B, D are true. Sets remove duplicate elements; a new outer list can be appended to independently.

questions.text: Select ALL appropriate actions when preparing a real-world dataset.
options: A. Check whether duplicate rows are accidental repeated records.
B. Automatically delete every unusual measurement.
C. Convert different measurement units to one consistent unit.
D. Investigate why some values are missing.
E. Check whether an apparent outlier could be a valid observation.
questions.explanation: A, C, D, E are appropriate. An unusual value needs investigation; automatic deletion can discard valid information.

questions.text: For the dataset 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, select ALL correct statements.
options: D. Adding 10 to every value leaves the range unchanged.
E. Doubling every value leaves the mean unchanged.
questions.explanation: Sum 25 gives mean 5; the middle value is 5; range is 9-2=7. Translation preserves range, whereas doubling values doubles their mean.

questions.text: Select ALL correct statements about algorithms and data structures.
options: A. Standard binary search relies on appropriately ordered data.
B. A queue normally removes the oldest waiting item first.
C. A stack normally removes the oldest item first.
D. Standard selection sort always makes exactly n^2 comparisons.
E. Five distinct items have 10 unordered pairs of different items.
questions.explanation: A, B, E are true. A stack uses LIFO. Standard selection sort compares n(n-1)/2 pairs; 5*4/2=10.

questions.text: Select ALL correct statements about machine learning.
options: A. K-Means needs a class label for every example.
B. The sigmoid in logistic regression outputs a value between 0 and 1.
C. Changing feature scales can change KNN distances and predictions.
D. Perfect training accuracy guarantees perfect test accuracy.
E. Linear regression is normally used to predict numerical quantities.
questions.explanation: B, C, E are true. K-Means is unsupervised; performance on training examples does not guarantee generalization.

questions.text: Select ALL appropriate practices for an AI classification project.
options: A. Fit learned scaling parameters using the training data only.
B. Repeatedly use the final test set to select the best model settings.
C. Inspect class-specific errors when one class is rare.
D. Provide human review for consequential decisions.
E. Assume removing one sensitive feature always guarantees fairness.
questions.explanation: A, C, D are appropriate. Test-set tuning leaks information; other features may act as proxies for a removed sensitive attribute.

questions.explanation: There are C(5,3)=10 equally likely three-counter subsets; C(3,2)*C(2,1)=6 are favorable. Alternatively, each of RRB, RBR, BRR has probability 1/5, giving 3/5.

questions.text:
This bubble sort stops after a pass with no swaps. What is printed?
```python
nums = [1, 3, 2, 4]
comparisons = 0
for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
    swapped = False
    for j in range(len(nums) - 1 - i):
        comparisons += 1
        if nums[j] > nums[j + 1]:
            nums[j], nums[j + 1] = nums[j + 1], nums[j]
            swapped = True
    if not swapped:
        break
print(comparisons)
```
questions.explanation: The first pass makes 3 comparisons and one swap. The second makes 2 comparisons and no swaps, so it stops at 5 comparisons.

questions.text: An unweighted KNN classifier uses Euclidean distance. For P=(0,0), the examples are (1,0):A, (0,2):B, (2,1):B, (-3,0):A. What happens when k changes from 1 to 3?
options: C. k=1 predicts A; k=3 predicts B.
D. k=1 predicts B; k=3 predicts A.
questions.correctAnswer: C. k=1 predicts A; k=3 predicts B.
questions.explanation: Squared distances are 1,4,5,9. The closest example is A, but the closest three vote A,B,B.

questions.text:
Eight examples have 4 positive and 4 negative labels. Compare two tree splits.
Split X: left 3 positive/1 negative; right 1 positive/3 negative.
Split Y: left 2 positive/0 negative; right 2 positive/4 negative.
Using Gini=1-p_positive^2-p_negative^2, choose the split with LOWER weighted child Gini.
options: A. X, because its weighted Gini is 3/8 and that is lower.
B. Y, because its weighted Gini is 1/3, below X's 3/8.
C. They tie at weighted Gini 3/8.
D. X, because its weighted Gini is 1/4.
E. Y, because its weighted Gini is 4/9 after weighting.
questions.correctAnswer: B. Y, because its weighted Gini is 1/3, below X's 3/8.
questions.explanation: X has two equal-sized children with Gini 3/8. Y has Gini (2/8)*0+(6/8)*(4/9)=1/3. The unweighted right-child impurity 4/9 is not Y's weighted result.

questions.text: Four fixed logistic-regression probability estimates are 0.35, 0.55, 0.70, and 0.90. Predict class 1 when p>=threshold. If only the threshold changes from 0.5 to 0.75, how many predictions change from class 1 to class 0?
questions.explanation: At 0.5 the last three are positive; at 0.75 only 0.90 is positive. The estimates 0.55 and 0.70 switch decisions; their probabilities do not change.

questions.text: Select ALL correct Python statements.
options: A. After b=a for a list a, both names refer to the same list.
B. a.copy() always creates independent copies of every nested mutable object.
C. not (True and False) evaluates to True.
D. Integer floor division always rounds toward zero.
questions.explanation: A, C, E are true. copy() is shallow. Floor division rounds downward, so -3//2=-2, rather than -1.

questions.text: A dataset can contain several records from the same student. Select ALL appropriate evaluation practices.
options: A. Fit a missing-value imputer using the training data only.
B. Fit a scaler on all data because it does not read class labels.
C. Keep records from the same student on the same side of a split when evaluating performance on new students.
D. Assume deleting every row with any missing value is always best.
E. Use validation data to choose a decision tree's depth.
questions.explanation: A, C, E prevent leakage or support model selection. Repeated students across splits can make new-student performance look too good. Full-data scaling can leak information; missingness should be investigated.

questions.text: Start with 2,4,6,8 and append the value 100. Select ALL correct statements.
questions.explanation: New sum is 120 across five values, so mean=24. Sorted middle value is 6; range=100-2=98. Before the append, median=(4+6)/2=5.

questions.text: Select ALL correct statements about counting and algorithmic reasoning.
options: A. There are 28 pairs of indices satisfying 0<=i<j<8.
B. Two separate full scans of n items make 2n item visits in total.
C. Doubling n multiplies an n^2 operation count by four.
D. A recursive countdown needs a stopping case and progress toward it to terminate for its intended inputs.
E. Binary search always works correctly on an unsorted list.
questions.explanation: A: 8*7/2=28. B: n+n=2n. C: (2n)^2=4n^2. D describes the base case and decreasing work. E is false because standard binary search relies on order.

questions.text: Select ALL correct statements about basic ML models.
options: A. Feature units can affect both KNN and K-Means when they use Euclidean distance.
B. Logistic regression can estimate a binary-class probability.
C. A decision-tree split can produce two pure children even if the parent has mixed labels.
D. The model with lower training MSE must have lower test MSE.
E. K-Means cluster numbers necessarily have the same meaning as known class labels.
questions.explanation: A, B, C are true. A feature can perfectly separate mixed labels. Training fit does not guarantee test performance; unsupervised cluster IDs have no fixed class meaning.

questions.text: Select ALL correct statements about evaluation and responsible AI.
options: A. A classifier can have 99% accuracy while missing every example of a rare class.
B. Removing the sensitive attribute guarantees a model is fair.
C. Collect only personal information needed for the task.
D. Evaluate whether data and errors are representative of the intended users.
E. Removing human oversight always makes AI decisions fairer.
questions.explanation: A, C, D are true. Majority-class predictions can hide minority failure. Proxy variables and biased data can preserve unfairness; human oversight can help detect and correct errors.

questions.text:

questions.text:
A logistic-regression model uses z=x1-x2-0.5 and p=1/(1+e^(-z)). Example A has x1=3,x2=1; example B has x1=1,x2=2. Use e^(-1.5) approximately 0.223 and e^(1.5) approximately 4.482. Predict class 1 if p>=threshold.
(a) Calculate both scores z. [2 points]
(b) Calculate both probabilities to three decimals. [2 points]
(c) Give both class predictions at thresholds 0.5 and 0.85. [2 points]
(d) Explain whether changing the threshold changes z, p, or only the decision when the inputs and model stay fixed. [2 points]
questions.correctAnswer:
A: z=1.5; p=1/1.223=0.818. B: z=-1.5; p=1/5.482=0.182.
Threshold 0.5: A is class 1, B is class 0. Threshold 0.85: both are class 0.
Only the class decision can change; the fixed scores and probability estimates do not.
questions.explanation: Marking follows the 2+2+2+2 allocation. For each of (a) and (b), award 1 per example. For (c), award 1 per complete threshold pair. Example B uses e^(-z)=e^(1.5), not e^(-1.5).


questions.explanation: Accept equivalent correct one-pass code. Marking: empty case and valid initialization 2; extend/reset current run and start 2; maintain best start/length and preserve the earliest tie 2; return the pair 1; correct output 1. Update the best only for a strictly longer run; equal neighboring values break a run.

questions.text:
A test set has 100 messages: 10 spam and 90 ordinary messages. The two classifiers make these predictions:
Model A: 0 spam correctly caught; 10 spam missed; 90 ordinary correctly accepted; 0 ordinary wrongly flagged.
Model B: 8 spam correctly caught; 2 spam missed; 80 ordinary correctly accepted; 10 ordinary wrongly flagged.
(a) Calculate each model's accuracy (all correct predictions / all messages). [2 points]
(b) Calculate each model's spam recall, defined as spam correctly caught / actual spam. [2 points]
(c) If catching spam is the main priority and flagged messages receive human review, which model is more suitable? Explain the trade-off. [2 points]
(d) Give one concrete privacy safeguard for the message text. [2 points]
questions.correctAnswer:
Accuracy: A=90%, B=88%. Spam recall: A=0%, B=80%.
Prefer B for the stated priority: it catches 8 spam messages rather than 0, while wrongly flagging 10 ordinary messages for human review.
Privacy example: restrict message-text access to authorized reviewers and remove unnecessary personal identifiers before analysis.
questions.explanation: Award 1 point per accuracy and per recall. For (c), 1 for B with the stated priority and 1 for the false-positive trade-off.
